lead: Syntax-driven semantic analysis gives every grammar rule a meaning attachment, so a parse tree computes the sentence's logical form as it combines words. The idea exists because meaning is productive: familiar parts in a new structure still make sense. It is used in database query front ends, question answering, and any system that turns an English sentence into a checkable formula. This chapter shows the attachments, the lambda notation that writes them, and how quantifier scope follows from the same machinery.
prereq: You need: Chapter 4.1 for first-order logic, and Unit 3 for CFG rules and parse trees.

blocks.text: Compositionality says the meaning of a sentence is a function of the meanings of its parts and the way they combine. Syntax-driven semantic analysis makes the second half precise: every context-free grammar rule carries a semantic attachment. The rule-to-rule hypothesis states that for every syntactic rule there is one semantic rule. Lexical rules give base meanings to words; phrase-structure rules say how child meanings combine.

A parse tree becomes a recipe. Leaves hold lexical meanings. Each internal node applies the attachment of its rule to the meanings of its children. For rule S → NP VP, the attachment is given below. Here [[X]] is the semantic value of node X.

blocks.where: [[X]] is the semantic value of node X; [[NP]] is a function that takes the VP meaning and returns a truth value.

blocks.text: The design exists because language is productive. A speaker understands a new sentence by combining familiar words in a familiar structure. Attaching meaning to rules also keeps grammar and semantics aligned: a change in syntax is a change in the combination rule, not a patch to a word list. Semantic features can carry agreement or countability; Unit 3 covers feature structures, so the main work here is done by attachments.

Lambda calculus is the notation for attachments. The term λx.Student(x) means the function that maps an entity x to true when x is a student. The λ binds x inside its body. An occurrence of x is bound if it sits under a λx; otherwise it is free. In λx.P(x,y), x is bound and y is free, so the term still waits for a value for y.
Application writes a function next to its argument: (λx.Student(x))(Ravi). Beta-reduction replaces every bound occurrence of x with the argument.

blocks.where: φ is the lambda body; a is the argument; φ[x := a] is the result of substituting a for x. Only bound occurrences change.

blocks.text: Types stop nonsense combinations. Let e be the type of an entity and t the type of a truth value. Student is e → t. Every is (e → t) → ((e → t) → t). Reads is e → (e → t), because it first takes the object and then the subject. If f has type A → B and a has type A, then f(a) has type B. Applying a quantifier to an entity is a type error.

items: Collect the semantic values of the children.
Check that each function's argument type matches.
Pass the result to the parent rule.

blocks.text: Determiners like every and a do not name an entity. They are generalized quantifiers. For a property P and a property Q, the two meanings are below. P is the noun meaning and Q is the verb-phrase meaning.

blocks.where: P is the property denoted by the noun; Q is the property denoted by the VP; x and y are bound entity variables.

blocks.text: Quantifier scope is not fixed by surface order. Every student reads a book allows two logical forms. Surface scope: ∀x(Student(x) → ∃y(Book(y) ∧ Reads(x,y))). Inverse scope: ∃y(Book(y) ∧ ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x,y))). The first says each student may have a different book. The second says one book is read by every student.

A fixed attachment order on a CFG produces one reading. To keep both, a system can use underspecification: store a scope constraint such as every outscopes a, or a outscopes every, without choosing. A later stage resolves the constraint using context. This delays the choice instead of losing it.

The pipeline is parser to parse tree, parse tree to attached meanings, beta-reduction to logical form, then a model checker or database query. Some systems use typed feature grammars, some use categorial grammar, some use dependency-to-logic rules. All share this parser-to-logical-form pipeline.

figure.caption: Each phrase node holds the meaning its rule builds from its children. The object NP joins reads to make the VP, and the subject NP is applied last, so ∀ ends up outside ∃: the surface reading.

spec.aria: A parse tree for Every student reads a book with a lambda meaning in every node: the determiners and nouns at the bottom, the subject NP and the VP in the middle, and the final logical form at S.

examples.question: Use the grammar S → NP VP; NP → Det N; VP → V NP; NP → Name. Lexical entries: every: λP.λQ.∀x(P(x) → Q(x)); student: λx.Student(x); a: λP.λQ.∃y(P(y) ∧ Q(y)); book: λy.Book(y); reads: λy.λx.Reads(x,y); Ravi: λP.P(Ravi). (a) Build the semantic attachment for 'Every student reads a book' and reduce it to a logical form. (b) Give the other reading the same words allow. (c) State the number of quantifiers, predicate symbols and bound variables in the first logical form.
steps: Parse tree: S[NP[Det every][N student]] [VP[V reads][NP[Det a][N book]]].
Subject NP: every applied to student gives (λP.λQ.∀x(P(x)→Q(x)))(λx.Student(x)) → λQ.∀x(Student(x)→Q(x)).
Object NP: a applied to book gives (λP.λQ.∃y(P(y)∧Q(y)))(λy.Book(y)) → λQ.∃y(Book(y)∧Q(y)).
VP: object NP applied to reads gives (λQ.∃y(Book(y)∧Q(y)))(λy.λx.Reads(x,y)) → λx.∃y(Book(y)∧Reads(x,y)).
S: subject NP applied to VP gives (λQ.∀x(Student(x)→Q(x)))(λx.∃y(Book(y)∧Reads(x,y))) → ∀x(Student(x)→∃y(Book(y)∧Reads(x,y))).
Other reading: let the object quantifier take wide scope: ∃y(Book(y)∧∀x(Student(x)→Reads(x,y))).
Counts in the first logical form: quantifiers ∀ and ∃ = 2; predicate symbols Student, Book, Reads = 3; bound variables x and y = 2.
examples.answer: The surface logical form is ∀x(Student(x) → ∃y(Book(y) ∧ Reads(x,y))), the inverse reading is ∃y(Book(y) ∧ ∀x(Student(x) → Reads(x,y))), and the first formula has 2 quantifiers, 3 predicate symbols and 2 bound variables.
examples.check:
quants = ["∀", "∃"]
preds = ["Student", "Book", "Reads"]
vars_ = ["x", "y"]
print(len(quants))
print(len(preds))
print(len(vars_))

traps: Attach meaning only to words, not to rules: then every student has no combination rule.
Apply λy.λx in the wrong order for a transitive verb: reads first wants the object, then the subject. Swapping gives Reads(book, student).
Treat quantifier scope as fixed by word order: Every student reads a book also allows one book for all students.
Skip type checking: applying a quantifier to an entity is a type error, not a bad style choice.
Substitute free variables during beta-reduction: only bound occurrences of the lambda variable change.

quiz.a: Every syntactic rule has a semantic rule; phrase-structure rules combine child meanings.

quiz.q: Why is every not the name of an entity?
quiz.a: It takes two properties and returns a truth value, quantifying over entities.

quiz.q: Which reading does the given attachment order produce for Every student reads a book, and why?
quiz.a: Surface scope ∀x(Student(x)→∃y(Book(y)∧Reads(x,y))), because the subject NP is applied last, outside the VP.
every expects e→t; book is e→t; the result is (e→t)→t, a quantifier meaning λQ.∀x(Book(x)→Q(x)).

quiz.q: How does underspecification delay quantifier scope?
quiz.a: It stores constraints without choosing an order; later context resolves which quantifier outscopes the other.

quiz.q: Given V = λy.λx.Likes(x,y) and object NP = λQ.∃z(Book(z)∧Q(z)), build the VP meaning.
quiz.a: Apply the object NP to V: λx.∃z(Book(z)∧Likes(x,z)).

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, syntax-driven semantics appears in spoken-language interfaces to databases, in semantic parsers that turn questions into SQL, and in compositional models that build phrase meanings from word vectors. Research moves from hand-written attachments to learned parsers that predict logical forms from data, and to underspecified representations that keep all readings until context resolves them. Search next for compositional distributional semantics, lambda calculus semantic parsing, quantifier scope underspecification, and abstract meaning representation.
